title: Review of c48's fuel-powered CIPS division: Supported. On fresh seed 2 the cells with fuel-charged enzyme turnover divide (6 persistent splits, generation 2, 0 merges; control 7), and a fuel fork at t=8000 removes all 16 bodies by t=8075 in both fork arms while the fed twin keeps 16
summary: Ran the finding's world unchanged on seed 2 (192^2, t=12000): 6 persistent splits, generation 2, 0 merges, 15 bodies at the end, first persistent split at t~3800, s membrane-like at the rim; fuel-independent control (react_const 1): 7 persistent splits, generation 2, 0 merges, first at t~3000. fork.py (the author's script, run from my directory with an identical copy of world.py): fork at t=8000, bodies 16 -> 17 -> 5 -> 0 at t=8000/8025/8050/8075 with reactivation kept fuel-dependent and 16 -> 17 -> 6 -> 0 with it switched to the fuel-independent rate at the fork; fed twin 16 at every check to t=8125 and 17 at t=8475. In the fuel-dependent fork arm the enzyme ends mostly inactive (e 0.033, i 0.117 at t=8475); in the constant-rate arm it stays active (e 0.120) yet the bodies still dissolve, so the bodies die for want of catalysis fuel, not of reactivated enzyme.

observations.D: pack_s2/sheet.png t=3100-11500: layered condensates pinch into daughters; lineage.png 6 persistent splits, generation 2, 0 merges; fork_s2.png: all bodies gone by t=8100-8200 in both fork arms, fed twin unchanged

controls_run.D: pack_const_s2/ (react_const 1, same seed); fork_s2.json fork and fork_const arms against fed

verdicts.limitation: Division is slower and slightly rarer with fuel-charged turnover (6 vs 7 splits, first split ~800 t later), as in the finding; generation 2 only in 12000 t. The fork shows that the bodies need fuel, but the constant-reactivation arm dies just as fast, so the fork does not isolate the turnover's own fuel dependence: the catalysis that makes the product also needs fuel. I did not rerun the moat or the reactivation budget.
